extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political science, comparative government, and history; educated general readers interested in American institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Expository treatment of the structure, origins, and practical workings of the United States' national and state governments, party system, public opinion, and related social/institutional forces, intended to explain their character and tendencies. Emphasises comparative perspective, historical context, and illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive multipart structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize the study into distinct parts addressing (I) the national government, (II) State governments and local government systems, (III) the party system and party organizations, (IV) public opinion and its expression, (V) illustrative instances from recent history and political questions outside party politics, and (VI) non-political institutions, society, and intellectual/spiritual forces relevant to the nation's character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author outlines Parts I–VI as necessary components; Parts III and IV receive extensive treatment (party system and public opinion). Use this multi-part plan to ensure both political machinery and broader social/ intellectual contexts are covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devote priority to public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat public opinion — the 'mind and conscience of the whole nation' — as central to understanding the American polity; describing leading political ideas, habits, and tendencies and showing how they express themselves in action is the most difficult and vital part of the task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate substantial chapters (the author assigns twelve) to sketch and analyze public opinion; recognize its cooler, larger-minded character relative to parties, and its decisive role in determining national policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrate general propositions with recent historical instances
rubrics_metrics.description: General descriptions and propositions about party systems and public opinion should be illustrated by instances drawn from recent American history and by discussions of political questions outside party politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and place illustrative cases (Part V) to give concreteness to general claims and to permit assessment of strengths and weaknesses of democratic government as actually practiced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer repetition to obscurity in exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: When necessary to trace a phenomenon to its source or to explain connections, the author will re-state material facts or re-enforce a view rather than risk obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should not hesitate to repeat information to aid readers who cannot be expected to retain all earlier material; clarity is prioritized over avoiding repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use outsider detachment advantageously but verify with natives
rubrics_metrics.description: A stranger (or Englishman) may notice salient features a native takes for granted and can maintain a position of detachment from party prejudice; however, this advantage should be balanced by consulting American friends and authorities to test views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First write down what strikes you as dominant facts, then corroborate by consulting native sources and friends; leverage outsider perspective for broad perspective but remedy unfamiliarity with local detail by reference to native authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain non-partisanship and avoid serving external party doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Strive to be non-partisan in describing politics; no fact should be stated or suppressed, and no opinion put forward, for the purpose of serving any foreign party-doctrine or furnishing arguments for use in external controversies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt detachment from party prejudice and beware of prepossessions in favour of persons, groups, constitutional dogmas, or national pretensions that can distort analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about causal attribution and overgeneralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid supposing that what the writer has seen or been told is generally true, and be cautious about assuming that current truths will continue; when tracing causes, inquire whether those causes are likely to be permanent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute less to single factors (e.g., form of government) than predecessors might; recognize complexity of causes and seek to determine facts and state problems correctly even when certainty is unattainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require parity of conditions before drawing comparative inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct inferences from the success or failure of a particular constitutional arrangement or political usage in another country are rarely sound because conditions differ; one must satisfy oneself that there is parity of conditions and surroundings before reasoning from ascertained results elsewhere to probable results at home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative examples cautiously, and explicitly test whether relevant circumstances are comparable before claiming transferability of institutional lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include succinct historical context to explain institutional origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a brief and plain outline of the events that gave birth to the Federal system and nurtured national feeling without extinguishing State feeling as a natural introduction to the present Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep historical digressions concise and targeted to explaining how present structures arose, avoiding needless deep historical detours while supplying necessary background for comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain complex institutional dualities clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Where institutions form dual systems (e.g., national and State governments), explain their distinct characters, overlapping authorities, and the devices that prevent clashes; stress the existence of 'two loyalties' and 'two governments' and the resulting complexity for students from other systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies (e.g., a large building incorporating smaller buildings) and clear comparisons (league vs. subdivisions) to convey how federal systems differ from leagues or unitary administrative divisions; highlight practical consequences for governance and political understanding.
